Grateful Dead at the Avalon Ballroom (Skeleton and Roses)

Alton Kelley and Stanley Mouse’s Family Dog poster of September 1966, which framed an old book illustration of a skeleton crowned with roses in banners of hand lettering.

Source
Victoria and Albert Museum: E.55-1999
Creator
Alton Kelley and Stanley Mouse
Made
1966 (concerts 16–17 September)
Style
Psychedelic art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Ornate, macabre, dense
Evidence
Downloaded the V&A image of object E.55-1999 (IIIF, 1200 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The imprint on this copy reads 26 (2), so it may be a second printing. The image is not stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A catalogues it as a psychedelic poster promoting the Grateful Dead and Oxford Circle at the Avalon Ballroom, offset lithography, 508 × 356 mm, by Alton Kelley and Stanley Mouse, San Francisco, 1966. V&A.

Wikipedia reports that Mouse and Kelley drew heavily on Art Nouveau graphics, in particular Alphonse Mucha and Edmund Joseph Sullivan, and credits the two with the skull-and-roses image for the Grateful Dead. Sullivan’s skeleton comes from a nineteenth-century edition of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám. Wikipedia: Stanley Mouse, Wikipedia: Alton Kelley.

Observed

  • A skeleton crowned and surrounded by red roses stands in a pale blue rectangle at the center. The drawing is fine black line with red and white roses.
  • GRATEFUL DEAD runs across a red ribbon at the top in black-outlined, swelling capitals. The ribbon ends curl down both sides and hold two Family Dog medallions.
  • SEPT 16 and SEPT 17 stand in large red script letters left and right of the image, symmetrically.
  • A blue cartouche at the bottom holds OXFORD CIRCLE in red and AVALON BALLROOM in blue on a white ribbon.
  • A bright blue border fills the space between the frames. Cream paper shows around the edge, and the ticket outlets at the bottom are set in plain type.

Why it belongs

The poster shows how much of the style is revival. The skeleton is Victorian book illustration, and the ribbons and medallions come from Art Nouveau and Victorian posters. The psychedelic part is the lettering and the crowding.

Its two-ink palette of red and blue is saturated but not vibrating, which is common in Family Dog posters.

Borrow

Frame a central image with a ribbon banner and mirrored side elements.

Set dates or secondary facts as large, symmetrical ornaments rather than small text.

Combine one fine-line illustration with heavy, swollen display lettering for contrast.
